title: Regional Voices
grammarNote: This lesson raises awareness of lexical variation across the Spanish-speaking world, anchored in Mexican Spanish (es-MX): work/job sets (chamba vs. curro vs. laburo), chatting verbs (platicar vs. charlar), vehicle and drink terms (carro/coche/auto, jugo/zumo), plus Mexican pragmatic markers (¿mande?, órale, sale y vale) and pragmatic diminutives (ahorita, tantito, un cafecito). It also builds receptive-only recognition of voseo (vos tenés) and peninsular vosotros forms, which learners should understand when they hear them but are not expected to produce.

phrases.target: Ando buscando chamba desde hace dos meses.
phrases.native: I've been looking for work for two months.
phrases.phonetic: AHN-doh boos-KAHN-doh CHAM-bah DES-deh AH-seh dohs MEH-ses
phrases.vocabularyIntro: 'Chamba' is the everyday Mexican word for 'job/work' — informal but extremely common in Mexico. Spain typically uses 'curro,' and much of South America (especially the Río de la Plata region) uses 'laburo' for the same idea; all three mean 'job' but are regionally specific and shouldn't be mixed.

exampleSentence.target: Por fin conseguí chamba en una empresa nueva.
exampleSentence.native: I finally got a job at a new company.

phrases.grammarNote: 'Chamba' functions as a regular feminine noun ('la chamba') and also gives rise to the verb 'chambear' ('to work') in Mexican Spanish.
phrases.memoryHook: Picture a busy 'champ' at work — 'chamba' rhymes with 'champ-a' and means the daily grind.

practiceItems.prompt: Translate: I've been looking for work for two months.
practiceItems.answer: Ando buscando chamba desde hace dos meses.

practiceItems.prompt: Ando buscando ___ desde hace dos meses.
¿Qué está buscando desde hace dos meses?

phrases.target: Oye, ¿podemos platicar un rato después de la junta?
phrases.native: Hey, can we chat for a bit after the meeting?
phrases.phonetic: OH-yeh, poh-DEH-mos plah-tee-KAHR oon RAH-toh des-PWES deh lah HOON-tah
phrases.vocabularyIntro: 'Platicar' is the standard Mexican verb for 'to chat/talk informally,' used constantly in daily life; 'charlar' means the same thing and is understood everywhere, but is more strongly associated with Spain and other regions.

exampleSentence.target: Nos quedamos platicando hasta muy tarde.
exampleSentence.native: We ended up chatting until very late.

phrases.grammarNote: 'Platicar' conjugates as a regular -ar verb (platico, platicas, platica...) and is interchangeable with 'hablar' or 'charlar' in casual Mexican speech.
phrases.memoryHook: 'Plática' (the noun) sounds like 'plot-ica' — imagine friends plotting out a friendly chat.

practiceItems.prompt: Translate: Hey, can we chat for a bit after the meeting?
practiceItems.answer: Oye, ¿podemos platicar un rato después de la junta?

practiceItems.prompt: Oye, ¿podemos ___ un rato después de la junta?
¿Qué le propone hacer después de la junta?

phrases.target: Dejé el carro en el estacionamiento de la oficina.
phrases.native: I left the car in the office parking lot.
phrases.phonetic: deh-HEH el KAH-rroh en el es-tah-syoh-nah-MYEN-toh deh lah oh-fee-SEE-nah
phrases.vocabularyIntro: 'Carro' is the everyday word for 'car' in Mexico (and much of the Caribbean/Andean region); 'coche' also works in Mexico but is the primary word in Spain, while 'auto' is more common in the Río de la Plata area — all three are understood everywhere but carry regional flavor.

exampleSentence.target: ¿Trajiste tu carro o vinimos en taxi?
exampleSentence.native: Did you bring your car, or did we come by taxi?

phrases.grammarNote: 'Carro' is a regular masculine noun ('el carro') with no irregularities — the regional variation is purely lexical, not grammatical.
phrases.memoryHook: 'Carro' sounds like 'carriage' — the modern-day version of a horse-drawn carriage.

practiceItems.prompt: Translate: I left the car in the office parking lot.
practiceItems.answer: Dejé el carro en el estacionamiento de la oficina.

practiceItems.prompt: Dejé el ___ en el estacionamiento de la oficina.

practiceItems.answer: Lo dejó en el estacionamiento de la oficina.

phrases.target: ¿Me traes un jugo de naranja, por favor?
phrases.native: Can you bring me an orange juice, please?
phrases.phonetic: meh TRAH-es oon HOO-goh deh nah-RAHN-hah, por fah-VOR
phrases.vocabularyIntro: 'Jugo' is the word for 'juice' throughout Latin America, including Mexico; 'zumo' is the word used in Spain for the same drink — both mean exactly the same thing, just split along a Spain/Latin America line.

exampleSentence.target: En esta fonda hacen un jugo de fruta buenísimo.
exampleSentence.native: At this diner they make a really good fruit juice.

phrases.grammarNote: 'Jugo' is a regular masculine noun ('el jugo') with no grammatical quirks; only the regional vocabulary choice (jugo vs. zumo) differs.
phrases.memoryHook: 'Jugo' sounds like 'juice-oh' — the '-oh' just tacks Spanish onto the English word you already know.

practiceItems.prompt: Translate: Can you bring me an orange juice, please?
practiceItems.answer: ¿Me traes un jugo de naranja, por favor?

practiceItems.prompt: ¿Me traes un ___ de naranja, por favor?

practiceItems.answer: Le pide un jugo de naranja.

phrases.target: ¿Mande? No escuché bien lo que dijiste.
phrases.native: Sorry, what? I didn't hear well what you said.
phrases.phonetic: MAHN-deh, noh es-koo-CHEH byen loh keh dee-HEES-teh
phrases.vocabularyIntro: '¿Mande?' is a distinctly Mexican way of politely asking someone to repeat themselves or answering when called — it comes from 'mande usted' ('command [me], sir/ma'am') and sounds far more courteous than a blunt '¿qué?'
phrases.grammarNote: '¿Mande?' historically comes from the imperative of 'mandar' ('to command') addressed formally, though today it's a fixed idiomatic response rather than a literal command.
phrases.memoryHook: Think of it as answering 'at your command?' — a small echo of old-fashioned courtesy still alive in Mexican speech.

practiceItems.prompt: Translate: Sorry, what? I didn't hear well what you said.
practiceItems.answer: ¿Mande? No escuché bien lo que dijiste.

practiceItems.prompt: ¿___? No escuché bien lo que dijiste.
¿Qué dice cuando no escucha bien algo?

phrases.target: Ahorita te marco, dame tantito para terminar esto.
phrases.native: I'll call you right now, give me just a little bit to finish this.
phrases.phonetic: ah-oh-REE-tah teh MAR-koh, DAH-meh tan-TEE-toh PAH-rah tehr-mee-NAHR EH-stoh
phrases.vocabularyIntro: 'Ahorita' (from 'ahora,' 'now') and 'tantito' (from 'tanto,' 'so much') are classic Mexican diminutives that soften time expressions — 'ahorita' can mean anywhere from 'right now' to 'in a little while' depending on tone, and 'tantito' means 'just a little bit.'

exampleSentence.native: Wait for me just a bit, I'm coming out right now.

phrases.grammarNote: The '-ito/-ita' diminutive suffix in Mexican Spanish often softens tone or shows affection rather than literally indicating small size — a key feature of MX pragmatics.

practiceItems.prompt: Translate: I'll call you right now, give me just a little bit to finish this.
practiceItems.answer: Ahorita te marco, dame tantito para terminar esto.

practiceItems.prompt: ___ te marco, dame tantito para terminar esto.

phrases.target: Sale y vale, nos vemos a las diez entonces.
phrases.native: Alright, sounds good, we'll see each other at ten then.
phrases.phonetic: SAH-leh ee VAH-leh, nohs VEH-mos ah lahs dyes en-TON-ses

phrases.target: ¿Nos tomamos un cafecito antes de la llamada?
phrases.native: Shall we grab a little coffee before the call?
phrases.phonetic: nohs toh-MAH-mos oon kah-feh-SEE-toh AHN-tes deh lah yah-MAH-dah

phrases.target: Perdón, no te entendí bien esa palabra que usaste.
phrases.native: Sorry, I didn't quite understand that word you used.
phrases.phonetic: pehr-DOHN, noh teh en-ten-DEE byen EH-sah pah-LAH-brah keh oo-SAS-teh

phrases.target: Aquí en México le decimos chamba al trabajo.
phrases.native: Here in Mexico we call work 'chamba.'
phrases.phonetic: ah-KEE en MEH-hee-koh leh deh-SEE-mos CHAM-bah al trah-BAH-hoh

phrases.target: Cada país tiene su propia manera de decir las cosas.
phrases.native: Every country has its own way of saying things.
phrases.phonetic: KAH-dah pah-EES TYEH-neh soo PROH-pyah mah-NEH-rah deh deh-SEER lahs KOH-sahs

dialogue.scenario: On a video call, Mexican, Spanish, and Argentine colleagues run into a regionalism that causes confusion.

turns.speaker: npc
turns.line: Hola a todos, ¿vosotros ya empezasteis con el curro de esta semana?
turns.native: Hi everyone, have you all already started this week's work?

turns.speaker: learner
turns.cue: Politely ask them to repeat what they said.
hints: ¿Mande? No escuché bien lo que dijiste
Perdón, no te entendí bien esa palabra que usaste

turns.speaker: npc
turns.line: Ah, perdón, preguntaba si ya empezaron el curro, el trabajo de esta semana.
turns.native: Oh sorry, I was asking if you'd already started the curro, this week's work.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.cue: Offer the Mexican equivalent of the word they used.
hints: Aquí en México le decimos chamba al trabajo
Ando buscando chamba desde hace dos meses

turns.speaker: npc
turns.line: Jaja, buenísimo. Yo igual ando con mucho laburo, ¿vos tenés algo urgente hoy?
turns.native: Haha, great. I'm also swamped with a lot of work — do you have anything urgent today?

turns.speaker: learner
turns.cue: Acknowledge that every country has its own way of saying things, then say you'll call them shortly.
hints: Cada país tiene su propia manera de decir las cosas
Ahorita te marco, dame tantito para terminar esto

turns.speaker: npc
turns.line: Bueno, entonces, ¿nos tomamos un café rápido antes de seguir con la reunión?
turns.native: Well then, shall we grab a quick coffee before continuing the meeting?

turns.speaker: learner
turns.cue: Agree to grab coffee, using the Mexican diminutive for it.
hints: ¿Nos tomamos un cafecito antes de la llamada?
